entries.3e903ae8e30a7075ac2a0c4a8c86e20d85ec996f: <div sID="gen13346" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Prov.2" sID="Prov.2"/> <div eID="gen13346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13347" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13348" type="x-p"/> Solomon, having foretold the destruction of those who are obstinate in their impiety, in this chapter applies himself to those who are willing to be taught; and, I. He shows them that, if they would diligently use the means of knowledge and grace, they should obtain of God the knowledge and grace which they seek, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.1-Prov.2.9">ver. 1-9</reference>. II. He shows them of what unspeakable advantage it would be to them. 1. It would preserve them from the snares of evil men (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.10-Prov.2.15">ver. 10-15</reference>) and of evil women, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.16-Prov.2.19">ver. 16-19</reference>. 2. It would direct them into, and keep them in, the way of good men, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.20-Prov.2.22">ver. 20-22</reference>. So that in this chapter we are taught both how to get wisdom and how to use it when we have it, that we may neither seek it, nor receive it in vain.
entries.d0a163719480c0ffb808dbc9875ed0aee8fa2398: <div eID="gen13348" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13347" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Search after Wisdom Encouraged.</title> <div sID="gen13349" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> My son, if thou wilt receive my words, and hide my commandments with thee; <hi type="super">2</hi> So that thou incline thine ear unto wisdom, <hi type="italic">and</hi> apply thine heart to understanding; 3 Yea, if thou criest after knowledge, <hi type="italic">and</hi> liftest up thy voice for understanding; <hi type="super">4</hi> If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as <hi type="italic">for</hi> hid treasures; <hi type="super">5</hi> Then shalt thou understand the fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and find the knowledge of God. <hi type="super">6</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> giveth wisdom: out of his mouth <hi type="italic">cometh</hi> knowledge and understanding. <hi type="super">7</hi> He layeth up sound wisdom for the righteous: <hi type="italic">he is</hi> a buckler to them that walk uprightly. <hi type="super">8</hi> He keepeth the paths of judgment, and preserveth the way of his saints. <hi type="super">9</hi> Then shalt thou understand righteousness, and judgment, and equity; <hi type="italic">yea,</hi> every good path. <div eID="gen13349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13350" type="x-p"/> Job had asked, long before this, <hi type="italic">Where shall wisdom be found? Whence cometh wisdom?</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.28.12">Job xxviii. 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.28.20">20</reference>) and he had given this general answer (<reference osisRef="Job.28.23">v. 23</reference>), <hi type="italic">God knoweth the place</hi> of it; but Solomon here goes further, and tells us both where we may find it and how we may get it. We are here told, <div eID="gen13350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13351" type="x-p"/> I. What means we must use that we may obtain wisdom. <div eID="gen13351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13352" type="x-p"/> 1. We must closely attend to the word of God, for that is the word of wisdom, <hi type="italic">which is able to make us wise unto salvation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.2.1-Prov.2.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. (1.) We must be convinced that the words of God are the fountain and standard of wisdom and understanding, and that we need not desire to be wiser than they will make us. We must <hi type="italic">incline our ear</hi> and <hi type="italic">apply our hearts</hi> to them, as to <hi type="italic">wisdom</hi> or <hi type="italic">understanding</hi> itself. Many wise things may be found in human compositions, but divine revelation, and true religion built upon it, are all wisdom. (2.) We must, accordingly, receive the word of God with all readiness of mind, and bid it welcome, even the commandments as well as the promises, without murmuring or disputing. <hi type="italic">Speak, Lord, for thy servant hears.</hi> (3.) We must hide them with us, as we do our treasures, which we are afraid of being robbed of. We must not only receive, but retain, the word of God, and lodge it in our hearts, that it may be always ready to us. (4.) We must incline our ear to them; we must lay hold on all opportunities of hearing the word of God, and listen to it with attention and seriousness, as those that are afraid of letting it slip. (5.) We must apply our hearts to them, else inclining the ear to them will stand us in no stead. <div eID="gen13352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13353" type="x-p"/> 2. We must be much in prayer, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.3">v. 3</reference>. We must <hi type="italic">cry after knowledge,</hi> as one that is ready to perish for hunger begs hard for bread. Faint desires will not prevail; we must be importunate, as those that know the worth of knowledge and our own want of it. We must cry, as new-born babes, after <hi type="italic">the sincere milk of the word.</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.2">1 Pet. ii. 2</reference>. We must <hi type="italic">lift our voice for understanding</hi> lift it up to heaven; thence these good and perfect gifts must be expected, <reference osisRef="Jas.1.17">Jam. i. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.38.34">Job xxxviii. 34</reference>. We must <hi type="italic">give our voice to understanding</hi> (so the word is), speak for it, vote for it, submit the tongue to the command of wisdom. We must consecrate our voice to it; having applied our heart to it, we must employ our voice in seeking for it. Solomon could write <hi type="italic">probatum est—a tried remedy,</hi> upon this method; he prayed for wisdom and so obtained it. <div eID="gen13353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13354" type="x-p"/> 3. We must be willing to take pains (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.4">v. 4</reference>); we must <hi type="italic">seek it as silver,</hi> preferring it far before all the wealth of this world, and labouring in search of it as those who dig in the mines, who undergo great toil and run great hazards, with indefatigable industry and invincible constancy and resolution, in pursuit of the ore; or as those who will be rich rise up early, and sit up late, and turn every stone to get money and fill their treasures. Thus diligent must we be in the use of the means of knowledge, following on to know the Lord. <div eID="gen13354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13355" type="x-p"/> II. What success we may hope for in the use of these means. Our labour shall not be in vain; for, 1. We shall know how to maintain our acquaintance and communion with God: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt understand the fear of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.5">v. 5</reference>), that is, thou shalt know how to worship him aright, shalt be led into the meaning and mystery of every ordinance, and be enabled to answer the end of its institution." <hi type="italic">Thou shalt find the knowledge of God,</hi> which is necessary to our fearing him aright. It concerns us to understand how much it is our interest to know God, and to evidence it by agreeable affections towards him and adorations of him. 2. We shall know how to conduct ourselves aright towards all men (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt understand,</hi> by the word of God, <hi type="italic">righteousness, and judgment, and equity,</hi> shalt learn those principles of justice, and charity, and fair dealing, which shall guide and govern thee in the whole course of thy conversation, shall make thee fit for every relation, every business, and faithful to every trust. It shall give thee not only a right notion of justice, but a disposition to practise it, and to render to all their due; for those that do not do justly do not rightly understand it." This will lead them in <hi type="italic">every good path,</hi> for the scripture will <hi type="italic">make the man of God perfect.</hi> Note, Those have the best knowledge who know their duty, <reference osisRef="Ps.111.10">Ps. cxi. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen13355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13356" type="x-p"/> III. What ground we have to hope for this success in our pursuits of wisdom; we must take our encouragement herein from God only, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.6-Prov.2.8">v. 6-8</reference>. <div eID="gen13356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13357" type="x-p"/> 1. God has wisdom to bestow, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.6">v. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Lord</hi> not only is wise himself, but he <hi type="italic">gives wisdom,</hi> and that is more than the wisest men in the world can do, for it is God's prerogative to open the understanding. All the wisdom that is in any creature is his gift, his free gift, and he gives it liberally (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.5">Jam. i. 5</reference>), has given it to many, and is still giving it; to him therefore let us apply for it. <div eID="gen13357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13358" type="x-p"/> 2. He has blessed the world with a revelation of his will. <hi type="italic">Out of his mouth,</hi> by the law and the prophets, by the written word and by his ministers, both which are his mouth to the children of men, <hi type="italic">come knowledge and understanding,</hi> such a discovery of truth and good as, if we admit and receive the impressions of it, will make us truly knowing and intelligent. It is both an engagement and encouragement to search after wisdom that we have the scriptures to search, in which we may find it if we seek it diligently. <div eID="gen13358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13359" type="x-p"/> 3. He has particularly provided that good men, who are sincerely disposed to do his will, shall have that <hi type="italic">knowledge and</hi> that <hi type="italic">understanding</hi> which are necessary for them, <reference osisRef="John.7.17">John vii. 17</reference>. Let them seek wisdom, and they shall find it; let them ask, and it shall be given them, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.7-Prov.2.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. Observe here, (1.) Who those are that are thus favoured. They are <hi type="italic">the righteous,</hi> on whom the image of God is renewed, which consists in righteousness, and those who <hi type="italic">walk uprightly,</hi> who are honest in their dealings both with God and man and make conscience of doing their duty as far as they know it. They are <hi type="italic">his saints,</hi> devoted to his honour, and set apart for his service. (2.) What it is that is provided for them. [1.] Instruction. The means of wisdom are given to all, but wisdom itself, <hi type="italic">sound wisdom,</hi> is laid <hi type="italic">up for the righteous,</hi> laid up in Christ their head, in whom <hi type="italic">are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,</hi> and who <hi type="italic">is made of God to us wisdom.</hi> The same that is the Spirit of revelation in the word is a Spirit of wisdom in the souls of those that are sanctified, that wisdom of the prudent which is to understand his way; and it is sound wisdom, its foundations firm, its principles solid, and its products of lasting advantage. [2.] Satisfaction. Some read it, He <hi type="italic">lays up substance for the righteous,</hi> not only substantial knowledge, but substantial happiness and comfort, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.21">Prov. viii. 21</reference>. Riches are things that are not, and those that have them only fancy themselves happy; but what is laid up in the promises and in heaven for the righteous will make them truly, thoroughly, and eternally happy. [3.] Protection. Even those who <hi type="italic">walk uprightly</hi> may be brought into danger for the trial of their faith, but God is, and will be, <hi type="italic">a buckler to them,</hi> so that nothing that happens to them shall do them any real hurt, or possess them with any terrific apprehensions; they are safe, and they shall think themselves so. <hi type="italic">Fear not, Abraham; I am thy shield.</hi> It is their way, the paths of judgment in which they walk, that the Lord knows, and owns, and takes care of. [4.] Grace to persevere to the end. If we depend upon God, and seek to him for wisdom, he will uphold us in our integrity, will enable us to <hi type="italic">keep the paths of judgment,</hi> however we may be tempted to turn aside out of them; for he <hi type="italic">preserves the way of his saints,</hi> that it be not perverted, and so preserves them in it safe and blameless to his heavenly kingdom. The assurances God has given us of his grace, if duly improved, will excite and quicken our endeavours in doing our duty. <hi type="italic">Work out your salvation,</hi> for <hi type="italic">God works in you.</hi>
entries.f3fbbaaa30dd58517f206cc505ef2dda61a03b5b: <div eID="gen13359" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Benefits Conferred by Wisdom.</title> <div sID="gen13360" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> When wisdom entereth into thine heart, and knowledge is pleasant unto thy soul; <hi type="super">11</hi> Discretion shall preserve thee, understanding shall keep thee: <hi type="super">12</hi> To deliver thee from the way of the evil <hi type="italic">man,</hi> from the man that speaketh froward things; <hi type="super">13</hi> Who leave the paths of uprightness, to walk in the ways of darkness; <hi type="super">14</hi> Who rejoice to do evil, <hi type="italic">and</hi> delight in the frowardness of the wicked; 15 Whose ways <hi type="italic">are</hi> crooked, and <hi type="italic">they</hi> froward in their paths: <hi type="super">16</hi> To deliver thee from the strange woman, <hi type="italic">even</hi> from the stranger <hi type="italic">which</hi> flattereth with her words; <hi type="super">17</hi> Which forsaketh the guide of her youth, and forgetteth the covenant of her God. <hi type="super">18</hi> For her house inclineth unto death, and her paths unto the dead. <hi type="super">19</hi> None that go unto her return again, neither take they hold of the paths of life. <hi type="super">20</hi> That thou mayest walk in the way of good <hi type="italic">men,</hi> and keep the paths of the righteous. <hi type="super">21</hi> For the upright shall dwell in the land, and the perfect shall remain in it. <hi type="super">22</hi> But the wicked shall be cut off from the earth, and the transgressors shall be rooted out of it. <div eID="gen13360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13361" type="x-p"/> The scope of these verses is to show, 1. What great advantage true wisdom will be of to us; it will keep us from the paths of sin, which lead to ruin, and will therein do us a greater kindness than if it enriched us with all the wealth of the world. 2. What good use we should make of the wisdom God gives us; we must use it for our own guidance in the paths of virtue, and for the arming of us against temptations of every kind. 3. By what rules we may try ourselves whether we have this wisdom or no. This tree will be known by its fruits; if we be truly wise, it will appear by our care to avoid all evil company and evil practices. <div eID="gen13361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13362" type="x-p"/> This wisdom will be of use to us, <div eID="gen13362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13363" type="x-p"/> I. For our preservation from evil, from the evil of sin, and, consequently, from the evil of trouble that attends it. <div eID="gen13363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13364" type="x-p"/> 1. In general (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.10-Prov.2.11">v. 10, 11</reference>), "When wisdom has entire possession of thee, it will <hi type="italic">keep thee.</hi>" And when has it an entire possession of us? (1.) When it has dominion over us. When it not only fills the head with notions, but <hi type="italic">enters into the heart</hi> and has a commanding power and influence upon that,—when it is upon the throne there, and gives law to the affections and passions,—when it <hi type="italic">enters into the heart</hi> as the leaven into the dough, to diffuse its relish there, and to change it into its own image—then it is likely to do us good. (2.) When we have delight in it, when knowledge becomes <hi type="italic">pleasant to the soul:</hi> "When thou beginnest to relish it as the most agreeable entertainment, and art subject to its rules, of choice, and with satisfaction,—when thou callest the practice of virtue, not a slavery and a task, but <hi type="italic">liberty</hi> and <hi type="italic">pleasure,</hi> and a life of serious godliness the most comfortable life a man can live in this world,—then thou wilt find the benefit of it." Though its restraints should be in some respects unpleasant to the body, yet even those must be pleasant to the soul. When it has come to this, with us, <hi type="italic">discretion shall preserve</hi> us and keep us. God keeps <hi type="italic">the way of his saints</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.8">v. 8</reference>), by giving them discretion to keep out of harm's way, to keep themselves that the wicked one touch them not. Note, A principle of grace reigning in the heart will be a powerful preservative both against corruptions within and temptations without, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.16">Eccl. ix. 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.18">18</reference>. <div eID="gen13364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13365" type="x-p"/> 2. More particularly, wisdom will preserve us, <div eID="gen13365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13366" type="x-p"/> (1.) From men of corrupt principles, atheistical profane men, who make it their business to debauch young men's judgments, and instil into their minds prejudices against religion and arguments for vice: "It will <hi type="italic">deliver thee from the way of the evil man</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.12">v. 12</reference>), and a blessed deliverance it will be, as from the very jaws of death, <hi type="italic">from the way</hi> in which he walks, and in which he would persuade thee to walk." The enemy is spoken of as one (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.12">v. 12</reference>), an <hi type="italic">evil man,</hi> but afterwards as many (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.13">v. 13</reference>); there is a club, a gang of them, that are in confederacy against religion, and join hand in hand for the support of the devil's kingdom and the interests of it. [1.] They have a spirit of contradiction to that which is good: They <hi type="italic">speak froward things;</hi> they say all they can against religion, both to show their own enmity to it and to dissuade others from it. They are advocates for Satan; they plead for Baal, and <hi type="italic">pervert the right ways of the Lord.</hi> How peevishly will profane wits argue for sin, and with what frowardness will they carp at the word of God! Wisdom will keep us either from conversing with such men or at least from being ensnared by them. [2.] They are themselves apostates from that which is good, and such are commonly the most malicious and dangerous enemies religion has, witness Julian (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">They leave the paths of uprightness,</hi> which they were trained up in and had set out in, shake off the influences of their education, and break off the thread of their hopeful beginnings, <hi type="italic">to walk in the ways of darkness,</hi> in those wicked ways which hate the light, in which men are led blindfold by ignorance and error, and which lead men into utter darkness. The ways of sin are ways of darkness, uncomfortable and unsafe; what fools are those that leave the plain, pleasant, lightsome paths of uprightness, to walk in those ways! <reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">Ps. lxxxii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.11">1 John ii. 11</reference>. [3.] They take a pleasure in sin, both in committing it themselves and in seeing others commit it (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.14">v. 14</reference>): They <hi type="italic">rejoice</hi> in an opportunity <hi type="italic">to do evil,</hi> and in the accomplishment and success of any wicked project. It is sport to fools to do mischief; nor is any sight more grateful to them than to see <hi type="italic">the frowardness of the wicked,</hi> to see those that are hopeful drawn into the ways of sin, and then to see them hardened and confirmed in those ways. They are pleased if they can discern that the devil's kingdom gets ground (see <reference osisRef="Rom.1.32">Rom. i. 32</reference>), such a height of impiety have they arrived at. [4.] They are resolute in sin (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.15">v. 15</reference>): Their <hi type="italic">ways are crooked,</hi> a great many windings and turnings to escape the pursuit of their convictions and break the force of them; some sly excuse, some subtle evasion or other, their deceitful hearts furnish them with, for the strengthening of their hands in their wickedness; and in the crooked mazes of that labyrinth they secure themselves from the arrests of God's word and their own consciences; for they are <hi type="italic">froward in their paths,</hi> that is, they are resolved to go on in them, whatever is said against it. Every wise man will shun the company of such as these. <div eID="gen13366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13367" type="x-p"/> (2.) From women of corrupt practices. The former lead to spiritual wickednesses, the lusts of the unsanctified mind; these lead to <hi type="italic">fleshly lusts,</hi> which defile the body, that living temple, but withal <hi type="italic">war against the soul.</hi> The adulteress is here called <hi type="italic">the strange woman,</hi> because no man that has any wisdom or goodness in him will have any acquaintance with her; she is to be shunned by every Israelite as if she were a heathen, and a stranger to that sacred commonwealth. A strange woman indeed! utterly estranged from all principles of reason, virtue, and honour. It is a great mercy to be delivered from the allurements of the adulteress, considering, [1.] How false she is. Who will have any dealings with those that are made up of treachery? She is a strange woman; for, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> She is false to him whom she entices. She speaks fair, tells him how much she admires him above any man, and what a kindness she has for him; but she <hi type="italic">flatters with her words;</hi> she has no true affection for him, nor any desire of his welfare, any more than Delilah had of Samson's. All she designs is to pick his pocket and gratify a base lust of her own. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> She is false to her husband, and violates the sacred obligation she lies under to him. He was <hi type="italic">the guide of her youth;</hi> by marrying him she chose him to be so, and submitted herself to his guidance, with a promise to attend him only, and forsake all others. But she has <hi type="italic">forsaken</hi> him, and therefore it cannot be thought that she should be faithful to any one else; and whoever entertains her is partaker with her in her falsehood. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> She is false to God himself: She <hi type="italic">forgets the covenant of her God,</hi> the marriage-covenant (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.17">v. 17</reference>), to which God is not only a witness, but a party, for, he having instituted the ordinance, both sides vow to him to be true to each other. It is not her husband only that she sins against, but her God, who <hi type="italic">will judge whoremongers and adulterers</hi> because they despise the oath and break the covenant, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.18">Ezek. xvii. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mal.2.14">Mal. ii. 14</reference>. [2.] How fatal it will prove to those that fall in league with her, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.18-Prov.2.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. Let the sufferings of others be our warnings. Take heed of the sin of whoredom; for, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The ruin of those who are guilty of it is certain and unavoidable, if they do not repent. It is a sin that has a direct tendency to the killing of the soul, the extinguishing of all good affections and dispositions in it, and the exposing of it to the wrath and curse of God and the sword of his justice. Those that live in forbidden pleasures are dead while they live. Let discretion preserve every man, not only from the evil woman, but from the evil house, for the <hi type="italic">house inclines to death;</hi> it is in the road that leads directly to eternal death; <hi type="italic">and her paths unto Rephaim,</hi> to the <hi type="italic">giants</hi> (so some read it), the sinners of the old world, who, living in luxury and excess of riot, were cut down out of time, and their foundation was overthrown with a flood. Our Lord Jesus deters us from sinful pleasures with the consideration of everlasting torments which follow them. <hi type="italic">Where the worm dies not, nor is the fire quenched.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Matt.5.28-Matt.5.29">Matt. v. 28, 29</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Their repentance and recovery are extremely hazardous: <hi type="italic">None,</hi> or next to none, <hi type="italic">that go unto her, return again.</hi> It is very rare that any who are caught in this snare of the devil recover themselves, so much is the heart hardened, and the mind blinded, by the deceitfulness of this sin. Having once lost their <hi type="italic">hold of the paths of life,</hi> they know not how to take hold of them again, but are perfectly besotted and bewitched with those base lusts. Many learned interpreters think that this caution against the <hi type="italic">strange woman,</hi> besides the literal sense, is to be understood figuratively, as a caution, 1. Against idolatry, which is spiritual whoredom. Wisdom will keep thee from all familiarity with the worshippers of images, and all inclination to join with them, which had for many ages been of such pernicious consequence to Israel and proved so to Solomon himself. 2. Against the debauching of the intellectual powers and faculties of the soul by the lusts and appetites of the body. Wisdom will keep thee from being captivated by the carnal mind, and from subjecting the spirit to the dominion of the flesh, that notorious adulteress which <hi type="italic">forsakes its guide,</hi> violates the <hi type="italic">covenant of our God,</hi> which <hi type="italic">inclines to death,</hi> and which, when it has got an undisturbed dominion, makes the case of the soul desperate. <div eID="gen13367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13368" type="x-p"/> II. This wisdom will be of use to guide and direct us in that which is good (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">That thou mayest walk in the way of good men.</hi> We must avoid the way of the <hi type="italic">evil man,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">strange woman,</hi> in order that we may walk in good ways; we must <hi type="italic">cease to do evil,</hi> in order that we may <hi type="italic">learn to do well.</hi> Note, 1. There is a way which is peculiarly the way of good men, the way in which good men, as such, and as far as they have really been such, have always walked. 2. It will be our wisdom to walk in that way, to ask for the good old way and walk therein, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.16">Jer. vi. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.12">Heb. vi. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.1">xii. 1</reference>. And we must not only walk in that way awhile, but we must keep it, keep in it, and never turn aside out of it: <hi type="italic">The paths of the righteous</hi> are the paths of life, which all that are wise, having taken hold of, will keep their hold of. "That thou mayest imitate those excellent persons, the patriarchs and prophets (so bishop Patrick paraphrases it), and be preserved in <hi type="italic">the paths of those righteous</hi> men who followed after them." We must not only choose our way in general by the good examples of the saints, but must also take directions from them in the choice of our particular paths; observe the track, and go forth by the footsteps of the flock. Two reasons are here given why we should thus choose:—(1.) Because men's integrity will be their establishment, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.21">v. 21</reference>. It will be the establishment, [1.] Of their persons: <hi type="italic">The upright shall dwell in the land,</hi> peaceably and quietly, as long as they live; and their uprightness will contribute to it, as it settles their minds, guides their counsels, gains them the good-will of their neighbours, and entitles them to God's special favour. [2.] Of their families: <hi type="italic">The perfect,</hi> in their posterity, <hi type="italic">shall remain in it.</hi> They shall dwell and remain for ever in the heavenly Canaan, of which the earthly one was but a type. (2.) Because men's iniquity will be their destruction, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.22">v. 22</reference>. See what becomes of <hi type="italic">the wicked,</hi> who choose the way of <hi type="italic">the evil man;</hi> they <hi type="italic">shall be cut off,</hi> not only from heaven hereafter and all hopes of that, but <hi type="italic">from the earth</hi> now, on which they set their affections, and in which they lay up their treasure. They think to take root in it, but they and their families <hi type="italic">shall be rooted out of it,</hi> in judgment to them, but in mercy to the earth. There is a day coming which <hi type="italic">shall leave them neither root nor branch,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.4.1">Mal. iv. 1</reference>. Let that wisdom then <hi type="italic">enter into our hearts,</hi> and be <hi type="italic">pleasant to our souls,</hi> which will keep us out of a way that will end thus.  <chapter eID="Prov.2"/> <div eID="gen13368" type="x-p"/>

entries.5b2d4455ebc684e3be2eaf881f177f0f9bbae24c: <div eID="gen23720" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23721" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23722" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23722" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23721" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23723" type="x-p"/> The teacher promises his pupil the highest advantages, if he will follow the dictates of wisdom, <reference osisRef="Pro.2.1-Pro.2.9">Pro 2:1-9</reference>. He shall be happy in its enjoyment, <reference osisRef="Pro.2.10">Pro 2:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Pro.2.11">Pro 2:11</reference>; shall be saved from wicked men, <reference osisRef="Pro.2.12-Pro.2.15">Pro 2:12-15</reference>; and from the snares of bad women, <reference osisRef="Pro.2.16-Pro.2.19">Pro 2:16-19</reference>; be a companion of the good and upright; and be in safety in the land, when the wicked shall be rooted out of it, <reference osisRef="Pro.2.20-Pro.2.22">Pro 2:20-22</reference>. <div eID="gen23723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23724" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23725" type="x-p"/> My son - Here the tutor still continues to instruct his disciple. <div eID="gen23725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23726" type="x-p"/> Hide my commandments with theel Treasure them up in thy heart, and then act from them through the medium of thy affections. He who has the rule of his duty only in his Bible and in his head, is not likely to be a steady, consistent character; his heart is not engaged, and his obedience, in any case, can be only forced, or done from a sense of duty: it is not the obedience of a loving, dutiful child, to an affectionate father. But he who has the word of God in his heart, works from his heart; his heart goes with him in all things, and he delights to do the will of his heavenly Father, because his law is in his heart. See <reference osisRef="Pro.3.3">Pro 3:3</reference>.
entries.b0ecebfab9ad1bb16ad082565e9c11fcb9be2baa: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23727" type="x-p"/> If thou seekest her as silver - How do men seek money? What will they not do to get rich? Reader, seek the salvation of thy soul as earnestly as the covetous man seeks wealth; and be ashamed of thyself, if thou be less in earnest after the true riches than he is after perishing wealth. <div eID="gen23727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23728" type="x-p"/> Hid treasures - The original word signifies property of any kind concealed in the earth, in caves or such like; and may also mean treasures, such as the precious metals or precious stones, which are presumptively known to exist in such and such mines. And how are these sought? Learn from the following circumstance: In the Brazils slaves are employed to scrape up the soil from the bed of the Rio Janeiro, and wash it carefully, in order to find particles of gold and diamonds; and it is a law of the state, that he who finds a diamond of so many carats shall have his freedom. This causes the greatest ardor and diligence in searching, washing out the soil, picking, etc., in order to find such diamonds, and the greatest anxiety for success; so precious is liberty to the human heart. This method of searching for gold and precious stones is alluded to in <reference osisRef="Pro.3.13-Pro.3.15">Pro 3:13-15</reference>. In this way Solomon wishes men to seek for wisdom, knowledge, and understanding; and he who succeeds finds the liberty of the children of God, and is saved from the slavery of sin and the empire of death.
entries.638d42974434575623f44e92f68cc0b3ef0feb54: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23729" type="x-p"/> He layeth up sound wisdom - תושיה tushiyah. We have met with this word in Job; see <reference osisRef="Job.5.12">Job 5:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.6.13">Job 6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.11.6">Job 11:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.12.16">Job 12:16</reference>. See especially the note on <reference osisRef="Job.11.6">Job 11:6</reference> (note), where the different acceptations of the word are given. <div eID="gen23729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23730" type="x-p"/> Coverdale translates, "He preserveth the welfare of the righteous." It is difficult to find, in any language, a term proper to express the original meaning of the word; its seems to mean generally the essence or substance of a thing, The thing itself - that which is chief of its kind. He layeth up What Is Essential for the righteous.
entries.5a5a8278a68f797200fed49f36620151b60550e2: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen23730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23731" type="x-p"/> Then shalt thou understand - He who is taught of God understands the whole law of justice, mercy, righteousness, and truth; God has written this on his heart. He who understands these things by books only is never likely to practice or profit by them.
entries.8e4f425c216ede87056562c009fd42a1e0ea8b8f: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen23731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23732" type="x-p"/> Discretion shall preserve thee - מזמה mezimmah. See on <reference osisRef="Pro.1.4">Pro 1:4</reference> (note). Here the word is taken in a good sense, a good device. The man invents purposes of good; and all his schemes, plans, and devices, have for their object God's glory and the good of man: he deviseth liberal things, and by liberal things he shall stand. Coverdale translates, "Then shall Counsel preserve thee." A very good translation, much better than the present.
entries.599725415cadab2981c6680c0bb91b6bdea23a61: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen23732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23733" type="x-p"/> The man that speaketh froward things - תהפכות tahpuchoth, things of subverston; from תפך taphach, to turn or change the course of a thing. Men who wish to subvert the state of things, whether civil or religious; who are seditious themselves, and wish to make others so. These speak much of liberty and oppression, deal greatly in broad assertions, and endeavor especially to corrupt the minds of youth.
entries.435d56dc2f0f6754c1536877368453c5782e733d: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen23733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23734" type="x-p"/> The stranger which flattereth with her words - החליקה hechelikah, she that smooths with her words. The original intimates the glib, oily speeches of a prostitute. The English lick is supposed to be derived from the original word.
entries.d7af31aa82c51ed55c8632abf5953346b128fa6a: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen23734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23735" type="x-p"/> Which forsaketh the guide of her youth - Leaves her father's house and instructions, and abandons herself to the public. <div eID="gen23735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23736" type="x-p"/> The covenant of her God - Renounces the true religion, and mixes with idolaters; for among them prostitution was enormous. Or by the covenant may be meant the matrimonial contract, which is a covenant made in the presence of God between the contracting parties, in which they bind themselves to be faithful to each other.
entries.a56fe8694f74475ae8617483f2c755978b9dea29: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen23736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23737" type="x-p"/> For her house inclineth unto death - It is generally in by and secret places that such women establish themselves. They go out of the high road to get a residence; and every step that is taken towards their house is a step towards death. The path of sin is the path of ruin: the path of duty is the way of safety. For her paths incline unto the dead, רפאים repheim, the inhabitants of the invisible world. The woman who abandons herself to prostitution soon contracts, and generally communicates, that disease, which, above all others, signs the speediest and most effectual passport to the invisible world. Therefore it is said,
entries.8fd2697f64b24c122c026073b5340fcbdd8f007f: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen23737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23738" type="x-p"/> None that go unto her return again - There are very few instances of prostitutes ever returning to the paths of sobriety and truth; perhaps not one of such as become prostitutes through a natural propensity to debauchery. Among those who have been deceived, debauched, and abandoned, many have been reclaimed; and to such alone penitentiaries may be useful; to the others they may only be incentives to farther sinning. Rakes and debauchees are sometimes converted: but most of them never lay hold on the path of life; they have had their health destroyed, and never recover it. The original, חיים chaiyim, means lives; not only the health of the body is destroyed, but the soul is ruined. Thus the unhappy man may be said to be doubly slain.
entries.199d82e3a6c0689a3d65fbf7b7f63bb7dd504290: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen23738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23739" type="x-p"/> That thou mayest mark - Therefore thou shalt walk.
entries.8afb97f884f80c7651adb4197f45cb18bf017b4c: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen23739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23740" type="x-p"/> Transgressors - בוגדים bogedim. The garment men, the hypocrites; those who act borrowed characters, who go under a eloak; dissemblers. All such shall be rooted out of the land; they shall not be blessed with posterity. In general it is so: and were it not so, one evil offspring succeeding another, adding their own to their predecessors' vices, the earth would become so exceedingly corrupt that a second flood, or a fire, would be necessary to purge it.  <chapter eID="Prov.2"/> <div eID="gen23740" type="x-p"/>

entries.7f71e2fef89b039961dbca178170789d29d6c028: <reference osisRef="Prov.2.1-Prov.2.2">Pro 2:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen10588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10589" type="x-p"/> The first אם, with that which it introduces, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.1">Pro 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.2">Pro 2:2</reference>, is to be interpreted as an exclamation, “O that!” (<hi type="italic">O si</hi>), and then as an optative, as <reference osisRef="Ps.81.9">Psa 81:9</reference>; Psa 139:19. אז ...כּי, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.3-Prov.2.5">Pro 2:3-5</reference>, with the inserted connecting clauses, would then be confirmatory, “for then.” But since this poet loves to unfold one and the same thought in ever new forms, one has perhaps to begin the conditional premisses with <reference osisRef="Prov.2.1">Pro 2:1</reference>, and to regard כּי אם as a new commencement. Hitzig takes this כי אם in the sense of <hi type="italic">imo</hi>: “much more if thou goest to meet her, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, by curious inquiry, not merely permittest her quietly to come to thee.” אם would then preserve its conditional meaning; and כּי as in <reference osisRef="Job.31.18">Job 31:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.130.4">Psa 130:4</reference>, since it implies an intentional negative, would receive the meaning of <hi type="italic">imo</hi>. But the sentences ranged together with אם are too closely related in meaning to admit such a negative between them. כּי will thus be confirmatory, not mediately, but immediately; it is the “for = yes” of confirmation of the preceding conditions, and takes them up again (Ewald, §356, b, cf. 330 b) after the form of the conditional clause was given up. The צפן, which in <reference osisRef="Prov.1.11">Pro 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.18">Pro 1:18</reference>, is the synonym of צפה, <hi type="italic">speculari</hi>, presents itself here, 1b, 7a, as the synonym of טמן, whence מטמנים, synon. of צפוּנים, <hi type="italic">recondita</hi>; the group of sounds, צף, צם, טם (cf. also דף, in Arab. dafan, whence dafynat, treasure), express shades of the root representation of pressing together. The inf. of the conclusion להקשׁיב, to incline (Gr. <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. ὡς ἀκροῷτο), is followed by the accus. of the object אזנך, thine ear, for הקשׁיב properly means to stiffen (not to purge, as Schultens, nor to sharpen, as Gesenius thinks); cf. under Psa 10:17. With חכמה are interchanged בּינה, which properly means that which is distinguished or separated, and תּבוּנה, which means the distinguishing, separating, appellations of the capacity of distinguishing in definite cases and in general; but it does not represent this as a faculty of the soul, but as a divine power which communicates itself as the gift of God (charisma).
entries.ea90567ded4e8b61ff84b598b6f7de0f430b94ea: <reference osisRef="Prov.2.3-Prov.2.8">Pro 2:3-8</reference> <div eID="gen10589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10590" type="x-p"/> Instead of כּי אם there is an old אל תקרי<note placement="foot">Regarding this formula, see Strack’s <hi type="italic">Prolegomena</hi>, pp. 66-70.</note> (read not so, but thus), כי אם (if thou callest understanding mother), which supposes the phrase כי אם (lxx) as traditional. If אם were intended (according to which the Targ. in the <hi type="italic">Bibl. rabbinica</hi>, but not in Norzi’s text, translates), then 3b would correspond; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.7.4">Pro 7:4</reference>, cf. Job 17:14. Thus: Yea, if thou callest for understanding, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, callest her to thee (<reference osisRef="Prov.18.6">Pro 18:6</reference>), invitest her to thee (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.15">Pro 9:15</reference>). The ק of בּקּשׁ is, with the exception of the imper. (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, בּקּשׁוּ), always without the <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi>. <reference osisRef="Prov.2.4">Pro 2:4</reference> belongs to the ideas in the Book of Job found in these introductory discourses, cf. <reference osisRef="Job.3.21">Job 3:21</reference>, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.2.14">Pro 2:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.3.22">Job 3:22</reference> (Ewald, Sprüche, p. 49). חפשׂ (חפּשׂ), <hi type="italic">scrutari</hi>, proceeds, as חפס shows, from the primary meaning of a ditch, and is thus in its root-idea related to חפר (to dig, search out). In the principal clause of <reference osisRef="Prov.2.5">Pro 2:5</reference> the 'יראת ה, as <reference osisRef="Ps.19.10">Psa 19:10</reference>, is the fear of Jahve as it ought to be, thus the reverence which is due to Him, the worshipping of Him as revealed. 'ה and אלהים are interchanged as קדשׁים and 'ה at Pro 9:10. דּעת is knowledge proceeding from practice and experience, and thus not merely cognition (<hi type="italic">Kenntnis</hi>), but knowledge (<hi type="italic">Erkenntnis</hi>). The thoughts revolve in a circle only apparently. He who strives after wisdom earnestly and really, reaches in this way fellowship with God; for just as He gives wisdom, it is nowhere else than with Him, and it never comes from any other source than from Him. It comes (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.6">Pro 2:6</reference>) מפּיו (lxx erroneously מפּניו ylsuoe), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, it is communicated through the medium of His word, <reference osisRef="Job.22.22">Job 22:22</reference>, or also (for λὀγος and πνεῦμα lie here undistinguished from one another) it is His breath (Book of Wisdom 7:25: ἀτμὶς τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ δυνάμεως καὶ ἀπόῤῥοια τῆς τοῦ παντοκράτορος δόξης εἰλικρινής); the inspiration (נשׁמת) of the Almighty (according to <reference osisRef="Job.32.8">Job 32:8</reference>) gives men understanding. In <reference osisRef="Prov.2.7">Pro 2:7</reference>, whether וצפן (Chethı̂b) or יצפּן (Kerı̂) is read, the meaning is the same. The former is the expression of the completed fact, as ἡτοίμασεν, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.9">1Co 2:9</reference>, and is rightly preferred by lxx and Syr., for one reluctantly misses the copula (since the thought is new in comparison with <reference osisRef="Prov.2.6">Pro 2:6</reference>). לישׁרם should be written with the accent <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi>. The Chokma-word (besides in Proverbs and Job, found only in Mic 6:9 and <reference osisRef="Isa.28.29">Isa 28:29</reference>) תּוּשׁיּה is a <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> formation (with the passing over of <hi type="italic">ô</hi> into <hi type="italic">û</hi>, as in תּוּגה) from הושׁה (whence the pr. names יושׁה and יושׁויה) = (Arab.) wasy and âsy, to re-establish, to advance, <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. of ישׁה = ושׁה, to stand, and thus means furtherance, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the power or the gift to further, and concretely that which furthers and profits, particularly true wisdom and true fortune.<note placement="foot">I was formerly in error in regarding the word as a <hi type="italic">Hophal</hi> formation, and in assigning to it the primary signification of being in a state of realized existence, of reality, in contradistinction to appearance only. The objection of J. D. Michaelis, Supplem. p. 1167, <hi type="italic">Non placent in linguis ejusmodi etyma metaphysica</hi>, etc., does not apply here, since the word is a new one coined by the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi>, but all the shades of meaning are naturally derived from the fundamental signification “furtherance” (cf. Seneca, <hi type="italic">Deus stator stabilitorque est</hi>). “תושׁיה, from Arab. âsy and wasy, to further by word and deed, to assist by counsel and act, to render help, whence the meanings <hi type="italic">auxilium</hi>, <hi type="italic">salus</hi>, and <hi type="italic">prudens consilium</hi>, <hi type="italic">sapientia</hi>, easily follow; cf. Ali’s Arab. proverb, “He furthers thee, who does not trouble himself about thee.”</note> <div eID="gen10590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10591" type="x-p"/> The derivation from ישׁ (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.21">Pro 8:21</reference>) is to be rejected, because “the formation would be wholly without analogy, so much the more because the י of this word does not represent the place of the ו, as is seen from the Arab. l-ys and the Syr. lyt” (Fl.);<note placement="foot">The Arab. ‛aysa (almost only in the negative la-ysa = לא ישׁ), of the same signification as ישׁ, with which the Aram. אית (איתי) is associated, presupposes an ‛âsa (= ‛âssa), to be founded, to found, and is rightly regarded by the Arabs as an old segolate noun in which the verbal force was comprehended.</note> and the derivation of ושׁה = שׁוה, to be smooth (Hitzig), passes over without any difficulty into another system of roots.<note placement="foot">The Arab. wsy and swy are confounded in common usage (Wetstein, Deutsch. Morgenl. Zeitschr. xxii. 19), but the roots וש and שו are different; וש and אש, on the contrary, are modifications of one root.</note> <div eID="gen10591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10592" type="x-p"/> In the passage under consideration (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.7">Pro 2:7</reference>), תּוּשׁיּה signifies advancement in the sense of true prosperity. The parallel passage 7a clothes itself in the form of an apposition: (He) a shield (מגן, <hi type="italic">n. instr</hi>. of גּנן, to cover) for הלכי תּם, pilgrims of innocence (Fl.), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, such as walk in the way (the object-accus., as <reference osisRef="Prov.6.12">Pro 6:12</reference>, for which in <reference osisRef="Prov.10.9">Pro 10:9</reference> בּ) of innocence. תּם is whole, full submission, moral faultlessness, which chooses God with the whole heart, seeks good without exception: a similar thought is found in Psa 84:12. לנצר, 8a, is such an <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. of consequence as להקשׁיב (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.2">Pro 2:2</reference>), and here, as there, is continued in the finite. The “paths of justice” are understood with reference to those who enter them and keep in them; parallel, “the way of His saints” (חסיד, he who cherishes חסד, earnest inward love to God), for that is just ארח־צדקה (<reference osisRef="Prov.12.28">Pro 12:28</reference>): they are הלכי צדקות (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.15">Isa 33:15</reference>). Instead of the <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>, the conjunctive <hi type="italic">Tarcha</hi> is to be given to ודרך.
entries.4c80f61a718506c10e1dd986bcdb4a03e01e26a4: <reference osisRef="Prov.2.9-Prov.2.11">Pro 2:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen10592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10593" type="x-p"/> With the אז repeated, the promises encouraging to the endeavour after wisdom take a new departure: 9 Then shalt thou understand righteousness, and justice,    And uprightness; every way of good. 10 For wisdom will enter into thine heart,    And knowledge will do good to thy soul; 11 Discretion will keep watch over thee,    Understanding will keep thee. <div eID="gen10593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10594" type="x-p"/> Regarding the ethical triad מישׁרים [righteousness, rightness], משׁפּט [judgment], and צדק [rectitude], <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Pro 1:3. Seb. Schmid is wrong in his rendering, <hi type="italic">et omnis via qua bonum aditur erit tibi plana</hi>, which in comparison with <reference osisRef="Isa.26.7">Isa 26:7</reference> would be feebly expressed. J. H. Michaelis rightly interprets all these four conceptions as object-accusatives; the fourth is the summarizing asyndeton (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.8.7">Psa 8:7</reference>) breaking off the enumeration: <hi type="italic">omnem denique orbitam boni</hi>; Jerome, <hi type="italic">bonam</hi>: in this case, however, טוב would be genitive (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.17.2">Pro 17:2</reference>). מעגּל is the way in which the chariot rolls along; in עגל there are united the root-conceptions of that which is found (גל) and rolling (גל). Whether כּי, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.10">Pro 2:10</reference>, is the argumentative “because” (according to the versions and most interpreters) or “for” (“<hi type="italic">denn</hi>,” J. H. Michaelis, Ewald, and others), is a question. That with כּי = “for” the subject would precede the verb, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.2.6">Pro 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.21">Pro 2:21</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Prov.1.32">Pro 1:32</reference> (Hitzig), determines nothing, as <reference osisRef="Prov.2.18">Pro 2:18</reference> shows. On the one hand, the opinion that כּי = “because” is opposed by the analogy of the כּי, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.6">Pro 2:6</reference>, following אז, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.5">Pro 2:5</reference>; the inequality between <reference osisRef="Prov.2.5-Prov.2.8">Pro 2:5-8</reference> and Pro 2:9. if the new commencement, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.9">Pro 2:9</reference>, at once gives place to another, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.10">Pro 2:10</reference>; the relationship of the subject ideas in <reference osisRef="Prov.2.10">Pro 2:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.11">Pro 2:11</reference>, which makes <reference osisRef="Prov.2.11">Pro 2:11</reference> unsuitable to be a conclusion from Pro 2:10. On the contrary, the promise not only of intellectual, but at the same time also of practical, insight into the right and the good, according to their whole compass and in their manifoldness, can be established or explained quite well as we thus read <reference osisRef="Prov.2.10">Pro 2:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.11">Pro 2:11</reference> : For wisdom will enter (namely, to make it a dwelling-place, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.33">Pro 14:33</reference>; cf. Joh 14:23) into thine heart, and knowledge will do good to thy soul (namely, by the enjoyment which arises from the possession of knowledge, and the rest which its certainty yields). דּעת, γνῶσις, is elsewhere fem. (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.6">Psa 139:6</reference>), but here, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.8.10">Pro 8:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.14.6">Pro 14:6</reference>, in the sense of τὸ γνῶναι, is masc. In <reference osisRef="Prov.2.11">Pro 2:11</reference> the contents of the אז תבין (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.9">Pro 2:9</reference>) are further explained. שׁמר על, of watching (for <reference osisRef="Job.16.16">Job 16:16</reference> is to be interpreted differently), is used only by our poet (here and at <reference osisRef="Prov.6.22">Pro 6:22</reference>). Discretion, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the capacity of well-considered action, will hold watch over thee, take thee under protection; understanding, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the capacity in the case of opposing rules to make the right choice, and in the matter of extremes to choose the right medium, will be bestowed upon thee. In תּנצרכּה, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.61.8">Psa 61:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.140.2">Psa 140:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.140.5">Psa 140:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.33.9">Deu 33:9</reference>, etc., the first stem letter is not assimilated, in order that the word may have a fuller sound; the writing  כּה for  ך is meant to affect the eye.<note placement="foot">For the right succession of the accents here, see <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 49, § 5; <hi type="italic">Accentuationssystem</hi>, xviii. § 3.</note>
entries.25c57e3797668560b0fd2db324d1742e3ff931c6: <reference osisRef="Prov.2.12-Prov.2.15">Pro 2:12-15</reference> <div eID="gen10594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10595" type="x-p"/> As in <reference osisRef="Prov.2.10">Pro 2:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.11">Pro 2:11</reference>, the אז תּבּין (“then shalt thou understand,” <reference osisRef="Prov.2.5">Pro 2:5</reference>) is expanded, so now the watching, preserving, is separately placed in view: 12 To deliver thee from an evil way,      From the man who speaks falsehood; 13 (From those) who forsake the ways of honesty      To walk in ways of darkness, 14 Who rejoice to accomplish evil,      Delight in malignant falsehood - 15 They are crooked in their paths,      And perverse in their ways. <div eID="gen10595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10596" type="x-p"/> That דּרך רע is not genitival, <hi type="italic">via mali</hi>, but adjectival, <hi type="italic">via mala</hi>, is evident from דרך לא־טוב, Pro 16:29. From the evil way, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, conduct, stands opposed to the false words represented in the person of the deceiver; from both kinds of <hi type="italic">contagium</hi> wisdom delivers. תּהפּכות (like the similarly formed תּחבּות, occurring only as plur.) means misrepresentations, viz., of the good and the true, and that for the purpose of deceiving (<reference osisRef="Prov.17.20">Pro 17:20</reference>), <hi type="italic">fallaciae</hi>, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, intrigues in conduct, and lies and deceit in words. Fl. compares Arab. ifk, a lie, and affak, a liar. להצּילך has <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, the constant servant of <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi>, instead of <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi>, according to rule (<hi type="italic">Accentssystem</hi>, vii. §2). העזבים (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.13">Pro 2:13</reference>) is connected with the collective אישׁ (cf. Jdg 9:55); we have in the translation separated it into a relative clause with the abstract present. The vocalization of the article fluctuates, yet the expression העזבים, like <reference osisRef="Prov.2.17">Pro 2:17</reference> העזבת, is the better established (<hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 53b); העזבים is one of the three words which retain their <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi>, and yet add to it a <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> in the tone-syllable (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., the two others, <reference osisRef="Job.22.4">Job 22:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.39.26">Job 39:26</reference>). To the “ways of honesty” (<hi type="italic">Geradheit</hi>) (cf. the adj. expression, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.9">Jer 31:9</reference>), which does not shun to come to the light, stand opposed the “ways of darkness,” the ἔργα τοῦ σκότους, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.12">Rom 13:12</reference>, which designedly conceal themselves from God (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.15">Isa 29:15</reference>) and men (<reference osisRef="Job.24.15">Job 24:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.38.13">Job 38:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.38.15">Job 38:15</reference>).
entries.a7e7c6a4ce46ae57b6769174dfd29ac012418617: <reference osisRef="Prov.2.16">Pro 2:16</reference> <div eID="gen10597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10598" type="x-p"/> With the resumption of להצּילך, the watchful protection which wisdom affords to its possessors is further specified in these verses: 16 To save thee from the strange woman,      From the stranger who useth smooth words; <div eID="gen10598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10599" type="x-p"/> The subject here continued is the fourfold wisdom named in <reference osisRef="Prov.2.10">Pro 2:10</reference>, Pro 2:11. זר signifies <hi type="italic">alienus</hi>, which may also be equivalent to <hi type="italic">alius populi</hi>, but of a much wider compass - him who does not belong to a certain class (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, the non-priestly or the laity), the person or thing not belonging to me, or also some other than I designate; on the other hand, נכרי, <hi type="italic">peregrinus</hi>, scarcely anywhere divests itself of the essential mark of a strange foreign origin. While thus אשּׁה זרה is the non-married wife, נכריּה designates her as non-Israelitish. Prostitution was partly sanctioned in the cultus of the Midianites, Syrians, and other nations neighbouring to Israel, and thus was regarded as nothing less than customary. In Israel, on the contrary, the law (Deu 23:18.) forbade it under a penalty, and therefore it was chiefly practised by foreign women (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.27">Pro 23:27</reference>, and cf. the exception, Rth 2:10),<note placement="foot">In Talmudic Heb. ארמית (Aramean) has this meaning for the Biblical נכריּה.</note> an inveterate vice, which spread itself particularly from the latter days of Solomon, along with general ungodliness, and excusing itself under the polygamy sanctioned by the law, brought ruin on the state. The <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi> contends against this, and throughout presents monogamy as alone corresponding to the institution and the idea of the relation. Designating marriage as the “covenant of God,” it condemns not only adulterous but generally promiscuous intercourse of the sexes, because unhallowed and thus unjustifiable, and likewise arbitrary divorce. Regarding the ancient ceremonies connected with the celebration of marriage we are not specially informed; but from <reference osisRef="Prov.2.17">Pro 2:17</reference>, Mal 2:14 (Ewald, Bertheau, Hitzig, but not Köhler), it appears that the celebration of marriage was a religious act, and that they who were joined together in marriage called God to witness and ratify the vows they took upon themselves. The perf. in the attributive clause אמריה החליקה proceeds on the routine acquired in cajoling and dissembling: who has smoothed her words, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, learned to entice by flattering words (Fl.).
entries.2f7451ad5c509996438c48ad0866f86900bfb879: Pro 2:17-19 7 Who forsakes the companion of her youth,      And forgets the covenant of her God; 18 For she sinks down to death together with her house,      And to the shadow of Hades her paths - 19 All they who go to her return not again,      And reach not the paths of life אלּוּף, as here used, has nothing to do with the phylarch-name, similar in sound, which is a denom. of אלף; but it comes immediately from אלף, to accustom oneself to a person or cause, to be familiar therewith (while the Aram. אלף, ילף, to learn, <hi type="italic">Pa</hi>. to teach), and thus means, as the synon. of רע, the companion or familiar associate (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Schultens). Parallels such as <reference osisRef="Jer.3.4">Jer 3:4</reference> suggested to the old interpreters the allegorical explanation of the adulteress as the personification of the apostasy or of heresy. <reference osisRef="Prov.2.18">Pro 2:18</reference> the lxx translate: ἔθετο γὰρ παρὰ τῷ θανάτῳ τὸν οἶκον αὐτῆς: she (the dissolute wife) has placed her house beside death (the abyss of death). This שׁחה [ἔθετο] is perhaps the original, for the text as it lies before us is doubtful, though, rightly understood, admissible. The accentuation marks בּיתהּ as the subject, but בּית is elsewhere always masc., and does not, like the rarer ארח, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.15">Pro 2:15</reference>, admit in usage a double gender; also, if the fem. usage were here introduced (Bertheau, Hitzig), then the predicate, even though ביתה were regarded as fem., might be, in conformity with rule, שׁח, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Isa 2:17. שׁחה is, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.44.26">Psa 44:26</reference>, 3rd pr. of שׁוּח, Arab. sâkh, to go down, to sink; the emendation שׁחה (Joseph Kimchi) does not recommend itself on this account, that שׁחה and שׁחח mean, according to usage, to stoop or to bend down; and to interpret (Ralbag, השׁפילה) שׁחה transitively is inadmissible. For that reason Aben Ezra interprets ביתה as in apposition: to death, to its house; but then the poet in that case should say אל־שׁאול, for death is not a house. On the other hand, we cannot perceive in ביתה an accus. of the nearer definition (J. H. Michaelis, Fl.); the expression would here, as 15a, be refined without purpose. Böttcher has recognised ביתה as permutative, the personal subject: for she sinks down to death, her house, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, she herself, together with all that belongs to her; cf. the permutative of the subject, <reference osisRef="Job.29.3">Job 29:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.23">Isa 29:23</reference> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., comm. <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>), and the more particularly statement of the object, <reference osisRef="Exod.2.6">Exo 2:6</reference>, etc. Regarding רפאים, shadows of the under-world (from רפה, synon. חלה, weakened, or to become powerless), a word common to the Solomonic writings, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Comment. on Isaiah</hi>, p. 206. What <reference osisRef="Prov.2.18">Pro 2:18</reference> says of the person of the adulteress, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.19">Pro 2:19</reference> says of those who live with her ביתה, her house-companions. בּאיה, “those entering in to her,” is equivalent to בּאים אליה; the participle of verbs <hi type="italic">eundi et veniendi</hi> takes the accusative object of the finite as gen. in <hi type="italic">st. constr</hi>., as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.12">Pro 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.2.7">Pro 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.23.18">Gen 23:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.9.10">Gen 9:10</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.10.20">Jer 10:20</reference>). The ישׁוּבוּן, with the tone on the ult., is a protestation: there is no return for those who practise fornication, (Note: One is here reminded of the expression in the <hi type="italic">Aeneid</hi>, vi. 127-129:<hi type="italic">Revocare gradum superasque evadere ad auras</hi>,<hi type="italic">Hoc opes, hoc labor est</hi>. <div eID="gen10599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10600" type="x-p"/> See also an impure but dreadful Talmudic story about a dissolute Rabbi, <hi type="italic">b. Aboda zara</hi>, 17a.) and they do not reach the paths of life from which they have so widely strayed.<note placement="foot">In correct texts ולא־ישיגו has the <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>. <hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 41; <hi type="italic">Accentuationssystem</hi>, xx. §2.</note>
entries.99b1c1b58b520a170b58a5dca61eb8bf90cc3849: <reference osisRef="Prov.2.20-Prov.2.22">Pro 2:20-22</reference> <div eID="gen10600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10601" type="x-p"/> With למען there commences a new section, coordinating itself with the להצּילך (“to deliver thee”) of <reference osisRef="Prov.2.12">Pro 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.16">Pro 2:16</reference>, unfolding that which wisdom accomplishes as a preserver and guide: 20 So that thou walkest in the good way,      And keepest the right paths. 21 For the upright shall inhabit the land,      And the innocent shall remain in it. 22 But the godless are cut off out the land,      And the faithless are rooted out of it. <div eID="gen10601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10602" type="x-p"/> Wisdom - thus the connection - will keep thee, so that thou shalt not fall under the seductions of man or of woman; keep, in order that thou... למען (from מען = מענה, tendency, purpose) refers to the intention and object of the protecting wisdom. To the two negative designations of design there follows, as the third and last, a positive one. טובים (contrast to רעים, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.19">Pro 14:19</reference>) is here used in a general ethical sense: the good (<hi type="italic">Guten</hi>, not <hi type="italic">Gütigen</hi>, the kind). שׁמר, with the object of the way, may in another connection also mean to keep oneself from, <hi type="italic">cavere ab</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.4">Psa 17:4</reference>); here it means: carefully to keep in it. The promise of <reference osisRef="Prov.2.21">Pro 2:21</reference> is the same as in the Mashal <reference osisRef="Ps.37.9">Psa 37:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.11">Psa 37:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.22">Psa 37:22</reference>; cf. Pro 10:30. ארץ is Canaan, or the land which God promised to the patriarchs, and in which He planted Israel, whom He had brought out of Egypt; not the earth, as <reference osisRef="Matt.5.5">Mat 5:5</reference>, according to the extended, unlimited N.T. circle of vision. יוּתרוּ (<hi type="italic">Milel</hi>) is erroneously explained by Schultens: <hi type="italic">funiculis bene firmis irroborabunt in terra</hi>. The verb יתר, Arab. watar, signifies to yoke (whence יתר, a cord, rope), then intrans. to be stretched out in length, to be hanging over (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Fleischer on <reference osisRef="Job.30.11">Job 30:11</reference>); whence יתר, residue, Zep 2:9, and after which the lxx here renders ὑπολειφθήσονται, and Jerome <hi type="italic">permanebunt</hi>. In 22b the old translators render יסּחוּ as the fut. of the pass. נסּח, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.63">Deu 28:63</reference>; but in this case it would be ינּסחוּ. The form יסּחוּ, pointed יסּחוּ, might be the <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. of סחח, but סחח can neither be taken as one with נסח, of the same meaning, nor with Hitzig is it to be vocalized יסּחוּ (<hi type="italic">Hoph</hi>. of נסח); nor, with Böttcher (§1100, p. 453), is יסּחוּ to be regarded as a veritable <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. יסּחוּ is, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.15.25">Pro 15:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.52.7">Psa 52:7</reference>, active: <hi type="italic">evellant</hi>; and this, with the subj. remaining indefinite (for which J. H. Michaelis refers to Hos 12:9), is equivalent to <hi type="italic">evellentur</hi>. This indefinite “they” or “one” (“<hi type="italic">man</hi>”), Fleischer remarks, can even be used of God, as here and <reference osisRef="Job.7.3">Job 7:3</reference> - a thing which is common in Persian, where <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, the expression rendered <hi type="italic">hominem ex pulvere fecerunt</hi> is used instead of the fuller form, which would be rendered <hi type="italic">homo a Deo ex pulvere factus est</hi>. בּוגדים bears (as בּגד proves) the primary meaning of concealed, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, malicious (treacherous and rapacious, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Isa 33:1</reference>), and then faithless men.<note placement="foot">Similar is the relation in Arab. of labbasa to libâs (לבוּשׁ); it means to make a thing unknown by covering it; whence telbı̂s, deceit, mulebbis, a falsifier.</note>  <chapter eID="Prov.2"/> <div eID="gen10602" type="x-p"/>

entries.e17355e17fe0452ea407d2d3ec97f3fa28a4e68c:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="2" type="chapter">

                  <ns0:p n="9">9.                   <ns0:p n="11">11. Discretion shall preserve thee <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">From wicked courses and the mischiefs which attend upon them, as is particularly expressed in the following Verses.</ns0:note>, understanding shall keep thee:</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="13">13. Who leave the paths of uprightness <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The way of God's Precepts.</ns0:note>, to walk in the ways of darkness <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
